The SEP also included significantly higher projections for economic growth in 2023 and slightly higher growth in 2024, alongside lower expected unemployment rates for both years. <3> The Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City held its 46th annual Economic Policy Symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, from August 24 to August 26, 2023. The theme for the 2023 symposium was "Structural Shifts in the Global Economy." As part of the event, Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell delivered a keynote speech on the economic outlook, titled "Inflation: Progress and the Path Ahead," on Friday, August 25, 2023. In his remarks, Powell stated that the Federal Reserve is prepared to raise rates further if appropriate to bring inflation down to its 2% goal. The speech and the full event agenda were announced in the days leading up to the symposium, and Powell's remarks were live-streamed on the Kansas City Fed's YouTube channel. <4> The Federal Reserve Board announced a $186 million fine against Deutsche Bank AG and its U.S. affiliates on July 19, 2023. [3] This penalty was imposed due to the bank's failure to adequately address persistent shortcomings in its anti-money laundering (AML) controls, which were previously identified in consent orders from 2015 and 2017. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] The Fed found that Deutsche Bank had made "insufficient remedial progress" on these earlier orders, which were related to its correspondent banking relationship with the Estonian branch of Danske Bank. [1, 2, 3] In addition to the fine, the Federal Reserve issued a consent order requiring Deutsche Bank to prioritize the completion of critical requirements from the prior orders and a written agreement to address broader deficiencies in its governance, risk management, and controls. The projected losses included over $100 billion from commercial real estate and residential mortgages and $120 billion from credit cards. Under the stress scenario, the aggregate common equity capital ratio was projected to decline by 2.3 percentage points to a minimum of 10.1 percent. Outcomes did vary across the banks, with some reports noting that midsize and regional banks fared worse than larger institutions. metadata.original_text: This time series records federal reserve data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2025-03-16 to 2025-06-01. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On February 7, 2025, the Federal Reserve released its semiannual Monetary Policy Report, which stated that the U.S. financial system is "sound and resilient." The report, submitted to Congress ahead of testimony from Fed Chair Jerome Powell, indicated that most banks maintain capital levels above regulatory requirements, though some continue to face significant fair value losses on fixed-rate assets. The report also noted that bank loan growth slowed in the second half of 2024. Furthermore, delinquency rates for commercial real estate loans and credit cards were described as elevated when compared to the period before the pandemic. <2> The Federal Reserve published the January 2025 Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS) on Bank Lending Practices on February 3, 2025. [1, 2, 3] The survey, which collected responses from 67 domestic banks and 20 U.S. branches of foreign banks, covered lending activity during the fourth quarter of 2024. [1, 3] Key findings indicate that while lending standards for commercial and industrial (C&I) loans tightened for firms of all sizes, there was stronger demand for these loans from large and middle-market companies. [1] Demand for C&I loans from small firms remained largely unchanged. [1] The report also noted expectations among bankers for lending standards to ease and for loan demand to strengthen across all categories during 2025. [1] <3> The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) held a meeting from January 28-29, 2025, with the subsequent policy rate decision announced on January 29, 2025. In line with standard procedure, the minutes from this meeting were released three weeks later, on February 19, 2025. The Federal Reserve Board's official calendar confirms these dates. <4> On December 4, 2024, six federal financial regulatory agencies and state financial regulators jointly issued a statement to address the growing issue of elder financial exploitation. [1, 7, 8] The participating federal agencies were the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (FRB), the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). [1, 3, 4] The statement provides supervised financial institutions with examples of risk management practices to identify, prevent, and respond to the illegal or improper use of an older adult's funds, but it does not impose new regulatory requirements. [1, 2] Highlighting the severity of the problem, a FinCEN analysis of Bank Secrecy Act reports for a one-year period ending in June 2023 found approximately $27 billion in suspicious activity linked to elder financial exploitation. [4, 8, 9] The guidance encourages institutions to develop effective oversight, train employees, use transaction holds where appropriate, establish trusted contact processes, file Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) with FinCEN, report to law enforcement and Adult Protective Services, and engage in consumer outreach. [4, 6, 9] <5> The Federal Reserve Board announced on November 22, 2024, that Princeton University had won the 21st annual College Fed Challenge. This competition encourages undergraduate students to deepen their understanding of the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System by analyzing economic and financial conditions to formulate a monetary policy recommendation. This year, 119 schools participated in the national competition. Harvard College secured second place, and the University of Virginia came in third. Honorable mentions were given to the University of Michigan, Pace University, and the University of Miami. <6> On November 22, 2024, the Federal Reserve Board announced the 2025 pricing schedule for payment services provided by Federal Reserve Banks to financial institutions like banks and credit unions, with the new rates effective January 1, 2025. The updated fees apply to services including the clearing of checks, Automated Clearing House (ACH) transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services. Overall, the changes are expected to result in an average price increase of 2.8% for established services, and the Federal Reserve anticipates recovering 104.1% of its actual and imputed expenses in 2025. Specific adjustments include increased fees for FedACH Services and Fedwire Funds Service. For the FedNow Service, fees will largely remain unchanged, with a notable modification to exclude charges for 'on-us' transactions that occur within the same financial institution. The board also released data showing growing adoption of the FedNow service. <7> The Federal Reserve Board released its semi-annual Financial Stability Report, concluding that the U.S. banking system is sound and resilient, with regulatory capital ratios near or exceeding historical highs. Despite this resilience, the report highlighted several vulnerabilities. It noted that valuation pressures remained elevated across a range of markets, including equities, corporate debt, and residential real estate, with the price-to-earnings ratio for equities near the top of its historical range. Additionally, liquidity in many financial markets was described as low, which could amplify the impact of shocks on asset prices. The report also incorporated findings from a survey on significant risks to financial stability, which gathered insights from academics, researchers, and market contacts between late August and late October 2024. <8> The Federal Reserve Board issued an order on November 21, 2024, prohibiting Shan Hanes, the former chief executive officer of Heartland Tri-State Bank in Elkhart, Kansas, from future participation in the banking industry. This enforcement action followed Hanes' embezzlement of $47.1 million of the bank's funds, which he diverted into a cryptocurrency scheme. This action directly led to the bank's insolvency and subsequent failure on July 28, 2023. In August 2024, Hanes had been sentenced to over 24 years in prison after pleading guilty to one count of embezzlement by a bank officer. His actions were described as a violation of his professional obligations and a betrayal of the trust placed in him, which jeopardized confidence in financial institutions. <9> The Federal Reserve Bank of New York published an article titled "The Financial Stability Implications of Digital Assets" in its November 2024 Economic Policy Review (Volume 30, Issue 2). [2, 3, 5, 6] The report provides an overview of financial stability risks associated with the rapidly growing digital asset ecosystem, adapting the Federal Reserve's traditional framework to this new domain. [2, 5] It identifies several vulnerabilities, including valuation pressures, funding risks, the use of leverage, and high interconnectedness within the crypto ecosystem. [2, 5, 6] The authors conclude that while these vulnerabilities exist, their contribution to systemic risk in the broader traditional financial system has been limited so far because the digital asset market is not yet a major provider of financial services and has limited connections to the traditional system. [2, 5]
